dhpak2.9:1.1: 2.9 The Story about the Elder Nigamavāsī Tissa
dhpak2.9:2.1: “A monastic who delights in heedfulness,” this Dhamma {1.283} [28.326] teaching was given by
dhpak2.9:2.2: the Teacher while he was in residence at Jetavana with reference to Elder Nigamavāsī Tissa.
dhpak2.9:3.1: For a youth of station, born and reared in a certain market town not far from Sāvatthī, went forth in
dhpak2.9:3.2: the dispensation of the Teacher. On taking his higher ordination, he became known as Nigamavāsī Tissa
dhpak2.9:3.3: (Tissa of the Market Town). He acquired the reputation of being frugal, content, secluded, energetic.
dhpak2.9:3.4: He always made his rounds for alms in the village where his relatives resided.
dhpak2.9:3.5: Although, in the neighboring city of Sāvatthī, Anāthapiṇḍika and other disciples were bestowing
dhpak2.9:3.6: abundant offerings and Pasenadi Kosala was bestowing Gifts beyond Compare, he never went to Sāvatthī.
dhpak2.9:4.1: One day the bhikkhus began to talk about him and said to the Teacher: “This bhikkhu Nigamavāsī Tissa,
dhpak2.9:4.2: constantly lives in intimate association with his kinsfolk. Although Anāthapiṇḍika and other disciples are
dhpak2.9:4.3: bestowing abundant offerings and Pasenadi Kosala is bestowing Gifts beyond Compare, he never comes to Sāvatthī.” {1.284}
dhpak2.9:5.1: The Teacher had Nigamavāsī Tissa summoned and asked him:
dhpak2.9:5.2: “Bhikkhu, is the report true that you are doing thus and so?”
dhpak2.9:5.3: – “Venerable Sir,” replied Tissa, “it is not true that I live in intimate association with my
dhpak2.9:5.4: relatives. I receive from these folk only so much food as I can eat. But after receiving so much food,
dhpak2.9:5.5: whether coarse or fine, as is necessary to support me, I do not go to Sāvatthī in search of more food,
dhpak2.9:5.6: thinking: ‘Why seek food?’ I do not live in intimate association with my relatives, venerable Sir.”
dhpak2.9:5.7: The Teacher, knowing the disposition of the bhikkhu, applauded him, saying: “Well done, well done, bhikkhu!”
dhpak2.9:5.8: and then addressed him as follows: “It is not at all strange,
dhpak2.9:5.9: bhikkhu, that after obtaining such a Teacher as I, you should be frugal.
dhpak2.9:5.10: For frugality is my tradition and my heritage.” And in response
dhpak2.9:5.11: to a request of the bhikkhus he related the following [28.327]
dhpak2.9:6.1: Once upon a time several thousand parrots lived in a certain
dhpak2.9:6.2: grove of fig trees in the Himālaya country on the bank of the Ganges.
dhpak2.9:6.3: One of them, the king-parrot, when the fruits of the tree in which he lived had
dhpak2.9:6.4: withered away, ate whatever he found remaining, whether shoot or leaf or bark,
dhpak2.9:6.5: drank water from the Ganges, and being very happy and contented, remained where he was.
dhpak2.9:6.6: In fact he was so very happy and contented that the abode of Sakka began to quake.
dhpak2.9:6.7: Sakka considered the cause, and seeing the parrot, determined to put him to the
dhpak2.9:6.8: test. Accordingly he employed his supernatural power and withered up the tree.
dhpak2.9:6.9: Straightaway the tree became a mere stump, full of holes and cracks. When the wind beat upon it,
dhpak2.9:6.10: there came forth from the tree a hollow sound, and out of the holes and cracks came forth dust.
dhpak2.9:6.11: {1.285} The parrot ate the dust, drank water from the Ganges, and going nowhere
dhpak2.9:6.12: else, remained perched on the top of the fig tree, reckoning nothing of wind and sun.
dhpak2.9:7.1: When Sakka observed how very happy and contented the parrot was, he said to himself: “I will go to him, let him
dhpak2.9:7.2: talk of the virtue of friendship, grant him his heart’s desire, and cause the fig tree to bear ambrosial fruit.”
dhpak2.9:7.3: Accordingly Sakka assumed the form of a royal goose, and
dhpak2.9:7.4: preceded by Sujā, the Asura maiden, went to the grove of fig trees,
dhpak2.9:7.5: alighted on the branch of a certain tree not far off, and entered
dhpak2.9:7.6: into conversation with the parrot by pronouncing the following verse:
dhpak2.9:8.1: “There are many green trees, Trees which have many fruits,
dhpak2.9:8.2: Why in this dry, hollow tree Does your mind find delight?”
dhpak2.9:10.1: When the Teacher had given this Dhamma teaching, he said: “At
dhpak2.9:10.2: that time Sakka was Ānanda, and the parrot-king was I myself.
dhpak2.9:10.3: Thus, bhikkhus, frugality is my tradition and my heritage.
dhpak2.9:10.4: It is, therefore, not at all strange that my son Nigamavāsī Tissa, having obtained such a teacher as I, is frugal.
dhpak2.9:10.5: A bhikkhu should be frugal, like Nigamavāsī Tissa. Such a bhikkhu is not liable to fall away from the
dhpak2.9:10.6: practices of calm and insight or from the [28.328] paths and the fruitions; rather he is nigh even unto Nibbāna.”
dhpak2.9:10.7: So saying, he pronounced the following verse:
dhpak2.9:11.1: A monastic who delights in heedfulness, seeing danger in
dhpak2.9:11.2: heedlessness, does not fall away: he is well-nigh to Nibbāna.
dhpak2.9:13.1: At the conclusion of the verse the Elder Nigamavāsī Tissa
dhpak2.9:13.2: attained Arahatship, together with the analytic knowledges,
dhpak2.9:13.3: and many others became Stream-enterers and so on,
dhpak2.9:13.4: and benefit arose to many people from the Dhamma teaching.
